lessons.title: Algorithms, Data Structures and Big O Notation
lessons.description: Understand algorithms, data structures, pseudocode, time complexity and space complexity.
lessons.content:
An algorithm is a finite, precise sequence of steps that transforms input into output. A data structure organizes values so operations such as access, insertion, deletion and searching can be performed efficiently. The best structure depends on the operations your program performs most often.

Algorithm design starts by defining inputs, outputs, constraints, edge cases and expected behavior. Pseudocode communicates the approach independently of programming language. A dry run manually traces each step for a sample input.

Time complexity describes how the amount of work grows as input size n increases; space complexity describes additional memory requirements. Big O gives an asymptotic upper bound, often used to discuss worst-case growth. Common growth classes are O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²) and O(2^n). Constants and lower-order terms are usually omitted when expressing asymptotic bounds.

One loop over n items is usually O(n). Two nested loops that each iterate n times are often O(n²). Halving the search space repeatedly yields O(log n). However, always count the actual iterations: nested loops do not automatically mean O(n²).

Distinguish input storage from auxiliary space. An algorithm that uses a fixed number of variables has O(1) auxiliary space; creating a second array of n elements uses O(n).

For interviews, state your approach, explain why it works, analyze time and space, and test empty inputs, duplicates, boundaries and large values.

lessons.title: Arrays, Strings and Traversal
lessons.description: Learn indexing, traversal, insertion costs, frequency counting and two-pointer techniques.
lessons.content:
An array stores an ordered sequence of elements. In many languages arrays occupy contiguous memory; Python lists are dynamic arrays of references. Index access is O(1), while searching an unsorted array is O(n). Inserting or deleting near the front of a dynamic array generally shifts elements and costs O(n). Appending is amortized O(1) for a dynamic array.

Traversal visits each element, often with a for loop. When tracking both index and value in Python, use enumerate(). A frequency map records how often each value occurs; dictionary lookups are average O(1), so a single pass can often build counts in O(n) expected time.

Strings represent sequences of characters. In Python strings are immutable: operations that produce a changed string return a new string. Building a result with a list of characters and ''.join(parts) is useful when many pieces must be combined.

Two pointers are indices that move through a sequence. Opposite-end pointers can check whether a string is a palindrome. Same-direction pointers can compact or filter elements. Sliding-window patterns track a contiguous segment, often avoiding repeated work.

Always define how to handle empty arrays, one-element arrays, repeated values and case sensitivity. For a palindrome that ignores punctuation and letter case, normalize the input before comparison.

Example interview tasks include finding a maximum, counting frequencies, reversing a string, checking palindromes and removing duplicates from a sorted array.

lessons.title: Searching Algorithms: Linear and Binary Search
lessons.description: Compare sequential searching with divide-and-conquer searching on sorted data.
lessons.content:
Searching finds whether an element exists and, often, its position. Linear search checks each element until a match is found or the collection ends. It works on unsorted data and has O(n) worst-case time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Binary search works on sorted data with random-access indexing. Compare the target with the middle element. If equal, return the index. If the target is smaller, search the left half; otherwise search the right half. Each comparison removes approximately half the candidates, yielding O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for the iterative form.

For an inclusive search interval [left, right], continue while left <= right and update right = mid - 1 or left = mid + 1. Forgetting these updates can cause an infinite loop.

A missing value should produce a documented result such as -1. If duplicate values exist, a basic binary search may return any matching position. To find the first occurrence, keep searching left after a match.

Binary search is not appropriate for arbitrary unsorted data. Sorting first costs additional time, usually O(n log n), and can change original positions.

When explaining a search, identify the precondition, invariant, termination condition and complexity. Practice both successful and unsuccessful searches.

lessons.title: Sorting Algorithms and Their Complexity
lessons.description: Understand bubble, selection, insertion and merge sort, including stability and complexity.
lessons.content:
Sorting arranges elements in an order, commonly ascending or descending. A stable sorting algorithm preserves the relative order of elements with equal keys. An in-place algorithm uses only a small amount of auxiliary storage, although implementations vary.

Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps those out of order. With an early-exit flag it can run in O(n) best-case time on sorted input, but O(n²) worst-case time.

Selection sort repeatedly selects the smallest remaining element and moves it into place. It performs O(n²) comparisons even for sorted input and the common swapping implementation is not stable.

Insertion sort maintains a sorted prefix and inserts each new value into its correct position. It is efficient for small or nearly sorted arrays: O(n) best-case and O(n²) worst-case time.

Merge sort recursively divides the array into halves and merges sorted halves. It takes O(n log n) time in the best, average and worst cases. Typical array-based merge sort requires O(n) additional space and is stable when ties are handled appropriately.

Python's built-in sorted() and list.sort() use Timsort, a stable sorting algorithm; prefer built-in sorting in production unless an interview specifically asks for implementation.

Compare algorithms using input size, available memory, stability requirements and whether data is nearly sorted. Always test duplicates, negative numbers, empty input and already sorted input.

examples.title: Insertion Sort
examples.explanation: Run this Python 3 example and examine its output and complexity.
examples.code:
def insertion_sort(values):
    result = values.copy()
    for i in range(1, len(result)):
        current = result[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and result[j] > current:
            result[j + 1] = result[j]
            j -= 1
        result[j + 1] = current
    return result

print(insertion_sort([7, 3, 5, 1, 3]))
print(insertion_sort([]))

lessons.title: Problem-Solving Patterns and Interview Practice
lessons.description: Combine complexity analysis, two pointers, hashing and step-by-step testing.
lessons.content:
Technical interviews assess reasoning, correctness, complexity and clear communication. Begin by restating the problem, asking about constraints and working through a small example. Identify whether the input is sorted, whether duplicates are allowed, and what to return when no solution exists.

A brute-force solution is often a useful starting point. For example, finding two numbers whose sum equals a target can be done with two nested loops in O(n²) time and O(1) extra space. A hash map can reduce expected time to O(n) at the cost of O(n) additional space.

For sorted arrays, a two-pointer solution can find a pair sum in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. For an unsorted array, a hash-based approach is usually easier.

Other common patterns include frequency counting, prefix sums, sliding windows, divide and conquer and sorting before processing. Do not apply a pattern blindly: verify its assumptions.

Write tests for empty input, no matching result, repeated elements, negative numbers and boundary cases. Distinguish returning values from printing them, and avoid mutating inputs unless required.

A clear interview explanation includes an example walkthrough, a short correctness argument, worst-case time and auxiliary-space analysis, and the reason you chose the data structure.

After solving a problem, review whether the solution handles duplicates correctly, whether it can be simplified and whether its complexity can be improved.

quizzes.question: What does an algorithm describe?
options: A finite sequence of steps for solving a problem
quizzes.explanation: An algorithm defines steps to transform input into output.

quizzes.question: Which complexity represents constant-time access?
quizzes.explanation: Constant-time operations do not grow with input size in the asymptotic model.

quizzes.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search on n elements?
quizzes.explanation: A missing target may require checking every element.

quizzes.question: Which condition must normally hold before applying binary search to an array?
options: The array must contain unique values
The array must have even length
The array must contain only positive numbers
quizzes.explanation: Binary search relies on ordering to discard half the candidates.

quizzes.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of iterative binary search?
quizzes.explanation: The search interval is halved after each comparison.

quizzes.question: Which operation is typically O(1) for an indexed dynamic array?
quizzes.explanation: Random-access indexing directly locates an array position.

quizzes.question: Which sorting algorithm usually has O(n log n) worst-case time?
quizzes.explanation: Merge sort divides and merges subarrays with logarithmic depth and linear work per level.

quizzes.question: What is the result of checking a palindrome using two pointers from both ends?
options: It can run in O(n) time with O(1) auxiliary space
quizzes.explanation: The pointers move inward once per character pair.

quizzes.question: Which statement about Python list.sort() is correct?
options: It always creates a new list
It sorts the list in place
quizzes.explanation: list.sort() mutates the existing list and returns None.

quizzes.question: For unsorted two-sum, what tradeoff does a hash map typically provide?
options: O(log n) time and O(1) space
O(n) expected time and O(n) space
quizzes.explanation: A dictionary stores previously visited values, enabling expected constant-time complement checks.

exercises.title: Analyze Algorithm Complexity
exercises.description: Explain the cost of common loops and array operations.
exercises.instructions: For each algorithm, identify worst-case time and auxiliary-space complexity: reading the first array element, summing all elements, two nested full-length loops and halving a positive integer until it reaches zero. Explain your reasoning and provide examples for n=8.

exercises.title: Array Maximum and Frequency Counter
exercises.instructions: Write Python functions maximum(values) and frequencies(values). maximum should return None for an empty list; frequencies should return a dictionary mapping each value to its count. Test empty lists, negatives and duplicates.

exercises.title: Implement Linear and Binary Search
exercises.instructions: Implement linear_search(values,target) for unsorted lists and binary_search(values,target) for sorted lists. Both return a matching index or -1. Explain preconditions and time complexity; test missing targets, duplicates, and empty lists.

exercises.title: Fix a Broken Binary Search
exercises.instructions: A binary search uses while left < right and, after a failed comparison, assigns left = mid or right = mid. Explain why this can miss the last candidate or loop forever. Rewrite it using an inclusive interval, correct updates and -1 when absent.

exercises.title: Implement Sorting and Two Sum
exercises.instructions: Implement insertion_sort(values) returning a new ascending list without modifying input. Then implement two_sum(values,target) returning indices of two distinct elements whose sum is target, or [] if none exist. Test duplicates, negatives, empty input and already sorted input. Explain worst-case time and auxiliary-space complexity.
